title: Adi bin Zayd and the Princess Hind

full_text:
Adi bin Zayd was an illustrious Christian Arab poet and diplomat of the kingdom of Al-Hirah on the Euphrates, renowned across Arabia and Persia for his handsome countenance, his courtly manners, and his mastery of verse.

During the spring festival of the Palm-Boughs, Adi visited the grand church of Al-Hirah, carrying a branch of flowering myrtle. Standing near the marble colonnade, his eyes met those of Princess Hind, the daughter of King Al-Nu'man. Hind was celebrated for her sharp intellect, her pride, and her refusal of all royal suitors who courted her with mere gold.

When Adi saw the princess, he recited an impromptu verse describing the sunrise over the river and how the purest blossom grows not in the king’s conservatory, but in the garden of the soul.

Hind listened, her heart stirred by the profound sincerity and spiritual elevation of his poetry. Rather than exchanging clandestine messages, Adi approached King Al-Nu'man openly, seeking her hand with dignity and honor.

Though political rivals sought to poison the king’s mind with false suspicions, Adi’s unblemished record as an ambassador to Constantinople and his unwavering fidelity won the monarch’s esteem.

King Al-Nu'man granted his consent, celebrating a wedding that united the desert tribes and the royal court in forty days of music and poetry. Their union became a proverb of enduring affection throughout Arabia, proving that verse spoken from the heart builds palaces that outlast earthly thrones.
moral: True love founded on poetic nobility, mutual respect, and patience creates a bond that bridges kingdoms.
